The Independent, published 18/19 Nov 2026

Exclusive: Three-quarters of companies said restoring membership would have the most positive impact – as Andy Burnham accuses Brexit ‘zombies’ of failing Britain

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

British businesses overwhelmingly back Britain to rejoin the EU, a major new consultation has found as Andy Burnham prepares for a crunch summit designed to undo some of the economic damage of Brexit.

In research shared exclusively with The Independent, three-quarters of firms said restoring EU membership would have the most positive impact on their business.

Just 10 per cent said they wanted to maintain the current approach of resetting relations with the bloc, which is moving too slowly to meet the scale of the challenges facing UK industry, the report by the UK Trade and Business Commission suggests.

It came as Mr Burnham, who has blamed Brexit for a decade of drift and division, hit out at Tory Brexiteer “zombies” who he said had refused to accept their deal with the EU had failed.

Speaking at Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs) on Wednesday, he told MPs the agreement due to be signed at the Brussels summit on Friday - which is expected to include deals on food and emissions trading, as well as a youth mobility agreement - could “bring growth to the British economy”.

But diplomats told the Guardian that the bloc would shut the door to discussions about its long-term relationship with the UK until the Government decides on reversing Brexit.

“Clarity is what we need more than anything from the UK. Don’t come back until you know what you want. Work out what your options really are and then come to negotiate,” one EU diplomat told the newspaper.

Business owners told the UKTBC rejoining the EU represented the “best outcome”, would see them “expand our growth” and would even solve “all” the post-Brexit problems they face.

They stressed that their biggest issues were the costs of Brexit and removing paperwork at the border, with one in three ranking this as their top priority. Freedom for the UK to set its own trade policy and regulation came bottom, with just four per cent and one per cent of companies picking them as top priorities respectively.

Steve Taylor, who owns Winterwood Farms Ltd in the South East of England, told the consultation that delays and cost “have meant that we no longer export soft fruit which has a shelf life of days, and paperwork can take a week to get. Previously we could agree a sale in the afternoon and the fruit would be in Holland overnight. Some of that fruit is now dumped.”

An analysis released earlier this year suggests almost every sector of the economy has been hit by Brexit, with exports of chemicals and pharmaceuticals down by 21 per cent since the UK left the EU, and those classed as “agrifood” down 29 per cent, according to researchers at the Centre for European Reform.

Nick Bloom, a professor at Stanford University, has also estimated that up to 8 per cent of GDP has been wiped off the UK economy through lost trade, increased red tape and delays in pushing the Brexit deal through, twice the official 4 per cent estimate from the Office for Budget Responsibility.

Peter Norris, Virgin Group chair and a member of the UKTBC, said that the research showed “it’s clear that far closer EU ties, including a conversation on membership, is now a crucial hygiene factor for success”.

“Firms need access to the European-wide funding and programmes that can take them to the next level, and they deserve the UK to have a seat at the table in deciding how EU rules are set. They’ve made their voices heard: it’s now vital the government listens,” he said.

We’re campaigning to rebuild Britain’s future in Europe

Former Labour leader Neil Kinnock described the findings from the report – which includes small and medium sized businesses, sole traders and major corporations – as “rational and patriotic”.

“They know that full re-connection with our largest, nearest market is vital for growth and prosperity,” he said. “Many were silent at the time of the referendum because they feared “political” involvement. They are now finding their voice and saying ‘join again’ to strengthen the stability, security and opportunity of our country.”

The consultation was launched after Mr Burnham’s announced that his government would consider different options for the UK-EU relations. He is expected to use the summit to start a conversation on the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with the EU, including potentially “going all the way” on membership.

For the survey, businesses’ views were sought on the current state of the trading relationship, and its possible future, weighing the benefits, trade-offs and risks.

Nearly 145 responses were received, from companies across the UK and of all shapes and sizes.

Lillian Jones, Labour MP and the chair of the UKTBC, an independent body of experts set up to track the impact of Brexit, including business leaders, cross-party parliamentarians and representatives from civil society, said: “Businesses told us that the closer our relationship with Europe, the more positive the impact for their business. Any future relationship should address the priorities and barriers they have raised, to deliver growth in every postcode.”

Mr Burnham branded Tory MPs “zombies” as he attacked the Brexit deal negotiated by Boris Johnson, which he said had made the country poorer and his party was improving.

“We heard from some of those zombies,” he said at PMQs, “but the truth is they don’t like it when we say the truth. The truth is the Brexit deal that they negotiated wasn’t good enough for Britain. It’s just a fact. The vast majority of the public know that as well.”

The Cabinet Office has been approached for comment.
